This was more to just highlight some of the observations we make about social stuff past a certain age. The best way to change your social life at an older age is to find different things to get involved with. Basically you need to put yourself into situations where other people might be seeking companionship. There is this phrase called "putting yourself in front of the storm". That pretty much captures what it is.

One of the things that is hard is each time you encounter a new group (a peer group or cohort in the formal terminology), you have a new opportunity to form social connections. That opportunity doesn't last forever, and you can fuck it up. If you enter a new group and routinely ignore subtle hints that someone wants to interact more, or you turn down invites places, pretty soon you are going to close doors. Most people don't recognize this, and don't take advantage of this narrow window where people are willing to build bridges with you. After a few times of not taking people up on invites, and not actively trying to involve yourself with a group of people, they'll take your cues and run with them and they'll stop trying. Then the opportunities won't come up, and it becomes really difficult to get back into that group once it's closed.

So here would be my advice to anyone trying to make new friends after the hyper-social years of high school and college:

  1. Find one or more interesting hobbies. Something you can learn. Something you can be passionate about, and something that will interest you enough to reliably get you out of your house or apartment to do it on a regular basis. There is one alternative to this (see #2).

  2. For those of you seeking a new job, your new group of co-workers will represent a similar opportunity. Transitioning into a new job is an option for some.

  3. Once you are there, be open to talking to people. I am not going to give you a primer here on the best ways to be sociable. But there are definitely ways and things to think about that can make talking to new people easier. But you need to present yourself and put yourself out there. People can't get connect with you if you don't give them something to connect to. If anyone is interested in this aspect of it all, shoot me a PM and I can go into more depth. But I am already ranting with this so I want to consolidate.

  4. At some point, there is going to be an opportunity that comes up. Be looking for it. It can be subtle. One HUGE MISTAKE people who want new friends often make is that they WAIT FOR EVERYTHING TO HAPPEN TO THEM. But here's the rub, most other people are also waiting for things to happen to them too. You might connect with someone on a similar interest in a particular band. Another person might say: "Oh, there's this little bar at the corner of blah and blah, and they have some really cool bands. We should do that sometime." Most of the time, people don't want to put themselves right in front of the possibility of rejection, so they'll cast these weak lures out. If someone says that, it means they want confirmation. MAKE SOMETHING HAPPEN. If someone indicates that interest, it means they think you are cool enough they'd spend time with you. So make it happen. Don't let that indicator just float away and die, because if you do, that person will internalize it as a form of rejection, even if they don't consciously think, "They told me no." But something in them will make them hesitate to do the same thing again. Make a fucking plan. Get your phone out. Look up a date, and say: "Hey this band is playing Friday, you guys wanna go catch the show and grab a few beers?"

  5. Likewise, if you are explicitly asked to do something with a new person or a new group, NEVER SAY NO to these opportunities for at least the first couple months of being around this new group. Obviously if you have legitimate schedule problems that prevent it, okay, but make it clear you are interested in hanging out but indicate why you cannot. But by and large, you have a critical window up front where you need to be AVAILABLE to saying yes to these invites.

  6. DO NOT FUCKING FLAKE OUT. People hate flakes. And again, even if it isn't on a conscious level, they are internalizing your flaking out as a subtle rejection. Just accept that. If you flake, it's no better than you saying, "You aren't as important to me as other people or things." You may have one more shot, or not shot after this for receiving another invite. Be available. It indicates your interest in someone or a group, that makes them feel good, feeling good will make them want you around.

  7. Be positive. Do not waste your first few exposures to people in these get togethers being too heavy, or too negative and associating yourself with bad feelings. Quiet people tend to get uncomfortable with this because they think it means they need to be the life of the party. NOT AT ALL. Most people have a more quiet person in their group, and it's all about the vibe. Myself personally, we have a guy in our group that doesn't say much, but it just doesn't feel right when he isn't around. It's because he smiles. He laughs. His energy is positive. Just be positive and don't complain, bitch about your life, or generally do shit that will bring people down. Just smiling and being warm will get you 95% of the way with most people. Also, if you laugh at their jokes they'll love you forever. On the other side of the token, don't be so desperate to create rapport that you freak people out. Just be chill.

Even just establishing one positive connection to a person inevitably opens you up to the rest of their social circle. It's a domino effect and it doesn't take long. But you have to put in the leg work up front by not saying no to people and being available and present for that shit to happen. Most people fuck up one of the things I mentioned, and its usually not taking initiative when one or more people drop hints that they want to do something with you, or they think they can avoid invites in the first few weeks and come out unscathed. If you say no and shut those opportunities down early, it's rare that people will open you like that again.

Concord Management and Consulting, LLC. - one of three businesses indicted by Mueller in February along with 13 individuals for election meddling, surprised the special counsel in April when they actually showed up in court to fight the charges. Mueller's team tried to delay Concord from entering the case, arguing that thee Russian company not been properly served, however Judge Dabney Friedrich denied the request - effectively telling prosecutors 'well, they're here.'

https://archive.is/q3gp1/d102b7a33a23dbcc093627f66609d10c5f4d4fb1.jpg

&nbsp

Concord was accused in the indictment of supporting the Internet Research Agency (IRA), a Russian 'troll farm' accused of trying to influence the 2016 US election.

On Thursday, Judge Freidrich asked Mueller's prosecutors if she should assume they aren't accusing Concord of violating US laws applicable to election expenditures and failure to register as a foreign agent.

Concord has asked Dabney to throw out the charges - claiming that Mueller's office fabricated a crime, and that there is no law against interfering in elections.

According to the judge’s request for clarification, the Justice Department has argued that it doesn’t have to show that Concord had a legal duty to report its expenditures to the Federal Election Commission. Rather, the allegation is that the company knowingly engaged in deceptive acts that precluded the FEC, or the Justice Department, from ascertaining whether they had broken the law. -Bloomberg

 

On Monday, Friedrich raised questions over whether the special counsel's office could prove a key element of their case - saying that it was "hard to see" how allegations of Russian influence were intended to interfere with US government operations vs. simply "confusing voters," reports law.com.

During a 90-minute hearing, Friedrich questioned prosecutor Jonathan Kravis about how the government would be able to show the Russian defendants were aware of the Justice Department and FEC’s functions and then deliberately sought to skirt them.

“You still have to show knowledge of the agencies and what they do. How do you do that?” Friedrich asked.

Kravis, a prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, argued that the government needed only to show that Concord Management and the other defendants were generally aware that the U.S. government “regulates and monitors” foreign participation in American politics. That awareness, Kravis said, could be inferred from the Russians’ alleged creation of fake social media accounts that appeared to be run by U.S. citizens and “computer infrastructure” intended to mask the Russian origin of the influence operation.

“That is deception that is directed at a higher level,” Kravis said. Kravis appeared in court with Michael Dreeben, a top Justice Department appellate lawyer on detail to the special counsel’s office. -law.com

 

Concord pleaded not guilty in May. Their attorney, Eric Dubelier - a partner at Reed Smith, has described the election meddling charges as "make believe," arguing on Monday that Mueller's indictment against Concord "doesn't charge a crime."
